aliases.name: Apparitio camatabodi
aliases.meaning: Pseudo-scientific binomial supplied by George B. Sudworth in Cox's 1910 book

description.summary: The Come-at-a-Body is a fearsome critter of early 20th-century American lumberjack folklore, described by William T. Cox in 1910 as a small, woodchuck-sized animal with soft kitten-like fur that suddenly charges out of the brush at New Hampshire travellers and stops abruptly inches away to startle them.
description.full: The Come-at-a-Body is one of the so-called 'fearsome critters' — comic, exaggerated tall-tale animals invented by lumberjacks of the North American logging frontier in the late 19th and early 20th centuries and committed to print in William T. Cox's Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods, With a Few Desert and Mountain Beasts (1910). According to Cox's informant, B. B. Bickford of Gorham, New Hampshire, the Come-at-a-Body is a small, woodchuck-like creature native to the White Mountains, covered in 'soft velvety fur like a kitten's', that practises a single, distinctive trick: it bursts from cover and charges directly at any passing traveller, then halts only inches away. Cox describes it as relying entirely on bravado and surprise — it does not bite, scratch, or harm — but the shock to a lone hiker, hunter, or mail-rider can be considerable. Like other fearsome critters (the hidebehind, the squonk, the hodag, the snallygaster), the Come-at-a-Body served lumber camps as both entertainment and a vehicle for hazing greenhorn workers. Coert Du Bois illustrated the animal for Cox's volume, and the U.S. Department of Agriculture forester George B. Sudworth supplied a tongue-in-cheek pseudo-Latin classification. The creature was reproduced and re-illustrated in Henry H. Tryon's 1939 anthology Fearsome Critters and again in modern reissues, securing the Come-at-a-Body a small but durable place in American lumberwoods folklore.

etymology.origin: Hiberno- and rural American English. 'Body' is a dialectal pronoun meaning 'a person' (as in 'a body could get hurt' = 'a person could get hurt'). The name 'Come-at-a-Body' literally describes the creature's habit: 'comes at a [person]'.
etymology.meaning: 'A creature that comes at a person'; named after its sole behaviour.
etymology.first_use: First in print in William T. Cox, Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods (Washington, D.C.: Judd & Detweiler, 1910).

features.description: Coat described by Cox's informant as 'soft and velvety like a kitten's'
Roughly the size and shape of a groundhog (woodchuck); compact, low-slung
Powerful short legs allow it to halt abruptly inches from a traveller
Cox notes the creature has no claws, fangs, or venom and relies entirely on bluff

physical.morphology: Small mammal of woodchuck/marmot proportions with disproportionately effective sprinting and braking abilities.

abilities.description: Bursts from concealment and runs straight at the nearest passer-by
Stops a few inches from the target without making contact, then retreats into cover
Conceals itself in low vegetation alongside trails and roads in the White Mountains

behavior.diet: Not specified by Cox; presumed forage of forest plants by analogy with woodchucks
patterns: Hides until a lone human approaches
Charges only at single travellers, never at groups
Returns to cover immediately after the charge
Reported chiefly to first-time travellers and mail-riders

range.description: Strictly localised to the White Mountains of northern New Hampshire in Cox's account, with secondary references in 20th-century compilations covering the wider Northern New England logging country.
regions: Maine and Vermont logging country (by extension in later compilations)

hotspots.name: Gorham, New Hampshire

location.description: Town at the northern edge of the White Mountains, given as B. B. Bickford's locale in Cox (1910)

hotspots.notes: Source community for the only original ethnographic account of the Come-at-a-Body.

first_recorded.source: William T. Cox, Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods, With a Few Desert and Mountain Beasts (1910)

peak_activity_periods.description: Heyday of the lumber-camp tall-tale tradition in the Northeastern United States
Henry H. Tryon's Fearsome Critters reprises Cox's bestiary, including the Come-at-a-Body
Reissues and digital reprintings keep the figure alive in cryptid- and folklore-enthusiast circles

temporal.seasonal_patterns: Implied by the lumberwoods context to be most active in the warm months when human travellers use the White Mountain trails.

origins.cultural_roots: North American lumber-camp oral culture of the late 19th and early 20th centuries: a tradition of comic 'tall-tale animals' invented to entertain weary loggers and to haze newcomers ('greenhorns') by convincing them of the existence of fanciful local fauna.
origins.earliest_accounts: First print attestation in Cox (1910), itself drawing on oral testimony from B. B. Bickford of Gorham, New Hampshire.
origins.folklore_connections: Belongs to the same body of fearsome-critter lore as the hidebehind, hodag, squonk, agropelter, axe-handle hound, splinter cat, sidehill gouger, and others; closely allied to the European wild-man and tall-tale traditions transplanted with northern European immigrants.

timeline.event: Publication of William T. Cox, Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods, including the Come-at-a-Body entry attributed to B. B. Bickford of Gorham, NH
timeline.significance: Sole original print attestation of the creature

timeline.event: Henry H. Tryon publishes Fearsome Critters, an expanded compilation that incorporates Cox's earlier entries
timeline.significance: Reinforces and extends the corpus of fearsome-critter tales

timeline.event: Reissues of Cox's book and online folklore catalogues bring the Come-at-a-Body back into print and onto the web
timeline.significance: Sustains the figure in modern cryptid- and folklore-enthusiast culture
timeline.source: Modern facsimile editions; A Book of Creatures and Cryptid Wiki online

history.modern_era: The Come-at-a-Body has no modern eyewitness tradition; it survives entirely as a literary fearsome-critter, regularly catalogued in popular folklore reference works and websites, occasionally illustrated in contemporary cryptid art, and used in classroom units on American tall tales and on logging-camp culture.

documentary.name: Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods (1910)
documentary.description: William T. Cox's entry on the Come-at-a-Body, citing B. B. Bickford of Gorham, NH, with illustration by Coert Du Bois.
documentary.analysis: The single primary source for the creature; everything later derives from this entry.
documentary.source: Cox, W. T. (1910), Fearsome Creatures of the Lumberwoods

documentary.description: Henry H. Tryon's compilation reproduces and extends the lumberwoods bestiary, drawing on Cox.

skeptical.name: Lumber-camp tall tale
skeptical.description: The Come-at-a-Body is a humorous fictional animal invented by loggers as a vehicle for entertainment and hazing rituals; it is not, and was never seriously claimed to be, a real biological organism.
evidence_cited: Stylistic features of the lumberwoods tall-tale tradition
The mock-Latin scientific name supplied by Sudworth
Absence of any independent eyewitness corpus

skeptical.name: Possible misidentification of woodchucks
skeptical.description: Some commentators suggest that the kernel of the joke draws on real, occasional aggressive bluff-charges by groundhogs (woodchucks) and other small mammals startled along trails.
evidence_cited: Cox's own description of the animal as 'woodchuck-like'

traditions: North American lumber-camp tall-tale tradition (late 19th – early 20th c.)
stories: The Come-at-a-Body of the White Mountains (Cox, 1910)
folklore.beliefs: Strictly humorous: the creature is offered as a deadpan local 'fact' designed to be believed only briefly by an inexperienced listener.
